implementation_notes: The class structure disappears: keep an append-only slice of {from time.Time; value} ordered by from and resolve the version in force by binary search - slices.BinarySearchFunc from Go 1.21 with a comparison that never returns 0 (giving the insertion point), or sort.Search from the earliest releases - then read the element one position to the left. time.Time is the Time Point and carries a location and an optional monotonic reading, so the collection must normalise to UTC or to civil date values on write. What replaces the classic structure: the slice plus one search function; the owner keeps a valueAt(when) method and a current() shortcut, and put() is an append (plus a sort, or a binary-search insertion where updates are frequent). The classic explicit range structure is only needed when validity can have gaps or overlaps, since a start-date-keyed slice cannot express 'no value in force' between two dates.
pitfalls: time.Time comparisons include the location and the monotonic clock reading: two values for the same instant in different locations are not equal, so keys must be normalised (UTC) or built from civil date components - and After/Before behave differently from Equal around DST.

Appending with append() reallocates the backing array: any slice header or element pointer handed out earlier no longer refers to the store, and concurrent reads during a write are a data race - guard the collection with a mutex or hand out copies.
A nil or empty history silently yields the zero value of the value type (0 cents, "" rate) unless the accessor returns an explicit ok boolean, as above.

Dates persisted as time.Time round-trip through the database with a location and precision that may differ from the in-memory value, so a lookup at an exact boundary (effective date midnight) can miss by microseconds; store and compare day-granularity values.
